old: \abstract{Streaming large language model (LLM) services can expose message-size metadata even when payloads are encrypted. We evaluate a fixed T5-based reconstructor in an instrumented, application-layer setting, using 300 aligned prompts for each of seven open-weight models and a 512-token generation limit. Saved term-frequency cosine scores (\texorpdfstring{$\phi$}{phi}) range from 0.030 to 0.568, with five models at 0.517--0.568. These are historical pipeline scores: an audit found that the archived line-based collector can discard token newline bytes, while the exact historical reconstruction inputs are unavailable in the supplied artifacts. References from TinyLlama and Phi-3.5-mini also exhibit missing word boundaries; those two series are retained as apparatus diagnostics and do not establish poor transfer to normally decoded responses. Victim responses reached end-of-sequence before the token limit in 0--65.7\% of cases. In separate 96-token pilots with 30 prompts per model, ordered logged traces exceeded shuffled, constant, and cross-prompt controls by 0.046--0.196 in mean \texorpdfstring{$\phi$}{phi}. These controls remove only selected trace features and do not isolate a pure language-prior baseline. Five framing transformations reduced frozen-reconstructor scores by 35.0--90.3\% in those pilots. A 512-token study with five decoder seeds and a prompt-disjoint maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) inverse included 3300 reconstructions; adaptation recovered much of the score lost under bucketing and batching. This study decoded only the first heuristic segment and scored it against the entire saved response. Both T5 input and output were limited to 80 tokens, so changes in segmentation and retained input also affect these comparisons. The results characterize a bounded reconstruction pipeline, rather than semantic disclosure, intrinsic model vulnerability, or attack success on encrypted transport traffic.}
new: \abstract{Streaming large language model (LLM) services can expose response-length metadata even when payloads are encrypted. We evaluate a fixed T5 reconstructor using validated application-layer byte-length traces from 300 aligned prompts for each of seven open-weight models. Complete reconstruction of 2100 archived responses under a 512-token victim budget yields mean term-frequency cosine scores ($\phi$) of 0.482--0.535 for five models. TinyLlama and Phi-3.5-mini retain malformed archived word boundaries and are analyzed as diagnostics. Separate generation of 300 responses per model with verified full-sequence detokenization yields mean scores of 0.435 and 0.504; these new cohorts are not pooled into the archived comparison. In 96-token pilots, replacing the trace by a constant reduces lexical scores for both tested models, while shuffling is significant only for Qwen after multiplicity correction; cross-prompt contrasts are inconclusive. Five framing transformations reduce frozen-reconstructor mean scores by 36.7--88.7\%. A 3300-reconstruction study with five decoder seeds and a prompt-disjoint maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) length inverse recovers much of the score lost under bucketing and batching. This study decodes the first heuristic segment against the full response; the primary experiment decodes all segments. Input and output limits of 80 T5 tokens make segmentation and retained encoder coverage part of each comparison. The results establish reproducible lexical behavior of this instrumented pipeline, without measuring semantic disclosure, intrinsic model vulnerability, or passive recovery from encrypted transport.}

old: This paper separates trace-based reconstruction from the recovery of a trace from encrypted production traffic. The intended laboratory observable is the ordered UTF-8 byte length of each token emitted by an instrumented service, before transport processing. This abstraction removes segmentation by HTTP and Transport Layer Security (TLS), buffering, retransmission, and multiplexing from the experiment. The implementation audit in Section~\ref{sec:measurement-audit}, however, identifies a mismatch between logged token lengths and the archived line-based collection path. We therefore distinguish the intended oracle from the saved historical pipeline results and from experiments that read token lengths directly from logs. No experiment here establishes passive extraction of event boundaries from encrypted traffic.
new: This paper separates reconstruction from a known length trace from extraction of that trace from encrypted traffic. The laboratory observable is the ordered UTF-8 byte length of each token fragment emitted by an instrumented service, before transport processing. A validated log oracle supplies these lengths and preserves newline bytes and empty fragments. This abstraction removes segmentation by HTTP and Transport Layer Security (TLS), buffering, retransmission, and multiplexing from the experiment. The historical line-collector discrepancy motivates the validation in Section~\ref{sec:measurement-audit}; all quantitative reconstruction results reported below use recorded, validated input vectors. No experiment here establishes passive extraction of event boundaries from encrypted traffic.

old: Building on Weiss \emph{et al.}, who reconstructed streamed responses from token-length patterns using a T5-based inversion pipeline~\cite{weiss2024prompt}, we examine one fixed reconstructor across open-weight victim models. Cross-model interpretation is conditional on collection provenance and reference decoding; the TinyLlama and Phi-3.5-mini series are treated as apparatus diagnostics.

The pilots and MAP study use different reconstruction scopes, so their baselines are not interchangeable. old: We evaluate a length-only reconstructor for an instrumented LLM service. The intended observation is the ordered byte length of each emitted token payload, with no access to the generating prompt, token identities, or victim-model internals. old: The historical harness emitted one separately decoded token payload per streaming write. Each write had the SSE-like byte serialization \texttt{data: \textless token\textgreater\textbackslash n\textbackslash n}; stream termination used \texttt{data: [DONE]\textbackslash n\textbackslash n}. Token text, token UTF-8 length, serialized-write UTF-8 length, and relative timestamp were logged. Per-run metadata included the model identifier, decoding parameters, prompt, concatenated emitted response, and token count. Raw newline characters within token text were not escaped, so a streaming write is not necessarily a single valid SSE data event. The reconstruction input used lengths only.
new: The instrumented harness associates each generated token position with a text fragment and records its UTF-8 length, serialized-write length, and relative timestamp. The historical implementation decoded each token independently; the new-generation implementation uses contextual prefix decoding and verifies that the fragments concatenate exactly to the full decoded token sequence. Each write has the SSE-like serialization \texttt{data: \textless fragment\textgreater\textbackslash n\textbackslash n}, and termination uses \texttt{data: [DONE]\textbackslash n\textbackslash n}. Raw newlines inside fragment text are not escaped, so a write is not necessarily a valid single SSE data event. The present experiments use validated lengths from the instrumented logs, not a line-based parser.

\subsection{Measurement and Reference-Text Audit}\label{sec:measurement-audit}
The archived collector used \texttt{requests.iter\_lines()} to split the incoming stream. Its implementation in \texttt{run\_validation.py} discarded empty lines and appended two newline bytes to each remaining line. Its inferred vector $X^{\mathrm{col}}$ therefore need not equal the logged payload vector $X^{\mathrm{log}}$. For example, the payload \texttt{:\textbackslash n\textbackslash n} has three bytes, but replay of this collector gives an inferred length of one. Replaying that implementation on the retained logs changes 2073 of 2100 vectors and the number of heuristic segments in 764 samples, despite matching the number of collected units in every sample. These are preprocessing-replay results, not archived historical T5 inputs. The exact primary input vectors and their binding to the collector version are unavailable in the supplied artifacts, so the replay does not establish which historical reconstructions were affected or how their scores would change. The reported primary scores are preserved; they must not be interpreted as results from a newly corrected common observation pipeline.

A separate audit concerns reference text. The historical harness decoded each token independently and concatenated the strings, without a demonstrated equivalence to decoding the complete token sequence. Of the stored references, 299/300 TinyLlama responses and 162/300 Phi-3.5-mini responses contain no ASCII space. This affects word-based evaluation and potentially the corresponding byte-length trace. Those two series are retained as apparatus diagnostics, not evidence of weak transfer on normally detokenized model responses. The observed counts do not determine how much of the score difference detokenization explains. Reliable replacement references require original token-sequence provenance or new generation with validated detokenization; inserting spaces heuristically would not recover ground truth.

The audit uses existing logs, recorded outputs, and local tokenizer resources without new victim generation or T5 inference. Its scripts and detailed outputs are retained under \texttt{reviews/ars\_electronics\_20261031/phase1\_panel/} in the accompanying repository. Subsequent code repairs replace line parsing with a validated log-length oracle and check received byte totals; this remains an instrumented observation, not passive transport extraction. The revised harness checks that context-aware token fragments concatenate to the full decoded response and records generated token IDs and provenance. These repairs do not retroactively validate archived outputs. Revalidation artifacts, including 2100 verified logged length vectors and separate reconstruction-run status files, are stored under \path{experiment_validation/revalidation_20261031/}; incomplete runs do not enter the manuscript's tables.
new:
\subsection{Measurement and Reference-Text Audit}\label{sec:measurement-audit}
The archived collector used \texttt{requests.iter\_lines()}, discarded empty lines, and appended two newline bytes to each remaining line. Its inferred vector $X^{\mathrm{col}}$ can differ from the logged vector $X^{\mathrm{log}}$: a fragment \texttt{:\textbackslash n\textbackslash n} contains three bytes, but this parser infers one. Replaying that implementation on the retained logs changes 2073 of 2100 vectors and the heuristic-segment count in 764 samples. These are preprocessing comparisons; the exact historical T5 input vectors and their binding to the old collector version were not retained.

The primary results below instead come from complete T5 inference on the 2100 validated logged vectors. This establishes the inputs used for the reported reconstructions without recovering undocumented historical inputs. Differences from older scores cannot be attributed solely to collection: the execution environment and reconstruction random-state handling also differ. The reconstructor is seeded after checkpoint loading so that cache initialization does not change a sample's random stream.

Reference text requires a separate check. The historical harness's independent token decoding produced no ASCII spaces in 299/300 TinyLlama responses and 162/300 Phi-3.5-mini responses. Those 600 archived references remain diagnostic; validating their emitted byte lengths does not restore their word boundaries. Historical token IDs are unavailable for all seven models, so complete-sequence detokenization of the other archived series is also not certified.

To evaluate the affected models with ordinary reference text, we generated 300 additional responses per model from the same prompts using contextual detokenization. All 600 passed exact agreement between concatenated fragments and full-sequence decoding, with token IDs, tokenizer and checkpoint provenance retained; all contain ASCII spaces. These new cohorts are reported separately. Current pinned checkpoint revisions, precision and placement are documented, but their identity with the historical execution is not established; the new results do not isolate a causal detokenization effect.

old: Victim-model decoding was deterministic, with temperature set to 0.0 and \texttt{top\_p} set to 1.0. For the primary cross-model analysis, a prespecified standardized subset was selected using the following shared parameters: $N=300$, \texttt{max\_new\_tokens}=512, \texttt{samples\_per\_segment}=3, \texttt{max\_sentences}=0 (all heuristic segments were reconstructed), and \texttt{num\_first\_candidates}=3. Six models used the instrumented one-token KV-cache loop, while Gemma-2-2B-it used greedy Hugging Face \texttt{model.generate()}. The same decoding parameters were applied in both cases. A sample was marked as end-of-sequence (EOS) complete when generation ended with an end-of-sequence token before reaching the 512-token limit (\texttt{finish\_reason=eos}, \texttt{response\_complete=true}). Length-truncated samples were retained in the primary $N=300$ comparison, while EOS-complete subsets were reported separately and were not treated as equivalent to truncated responses.
new: Victim-model decoding used greedy selection, with temperature 0.0 and \texttt{top\_p}=1.0. The primary cohort contains $N=300$ archived responses per model generated with \texttt{max\_new\_tokens}=512. Each reconstruction requests all heuristic segments (\texttt{max\_sentences}=0), samples three candidates per segment, and retains up to three first-segment candidates. Six historical victim models used a one-token KV-cache loop, while Gemma-2-2B-it used greedy Hugging Face \texttt{model.generate()}. Responses reaching EOS before the limit are marked \texttt{response\_complete}; length-truncated responses remain in the primary analysis. EOS-complete subsets are descriptive subsets, not interchangeable samples.

The evaluated models are listed in Table~\ref{tab:model_metadata}. Six are instruction- or chat-tuned; Phi-1.5 is a base-model stress test and does not identify a general base-versus-instruction effect~\cite{qwen25report,llama3report,llama32blog,gemma2report,phi15report,tinyllama2024,phi3report}. Reconstruction for every cohort uses float32 T5 checkpoints on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 Ti Laptop GPU with 8 GB VRAM, PyTorch 2.5.1 and Transformers 4.46.3. old: Reconstruction quality was computed using four lexical criteria against the stored emitted response $R$. The reported Levenshtein value is $\texttt{ed\_norm}=d(R,\widehat{R})/|R|$, where character length $|R|$ is the denominator; it can therefore exceed 1 when the reconstruction is much longer than the reference~\cite{levenshtein1966binary}. ROUGE-1 precision and ROUGE-L precision quantify unigram and longest-common-subsequence overlap~\cite{lin2004rouge}. The primary metric, $\phi$, is cosine similarity between unweighted, case-normalized term-frequency vectors of the reference and reconstruction~\cite{salton1975vector}. Terms are lowercase runs matching \texttt{[A-Za-z0-9']+}; punctuation can still delimit terms when spaces are absent. The cosine score was recomputed from stored texts for all 2100 samples to avoid mixing scoring backends. This recalculation verifies consistency of the lexical metric, not the collector or reference detokenization. For the MAP study, $\widehat{R}$ is the first heuristic segment's reconstruction and $R$ remains the entire stored response; this is a first-segment-to-full-response score, not first-sentence accuracy.
new: Reconstruction quality was computed against the complete reference response $R$ using four lexical criteria. The normalized Levenshtein value is $\texttt{ed\_norm}=d(R,\widehat{R})/|R|$, using reference character length as the denominator; it can exceed 1 when the prediction is much longer than the reference~\cite{levenshtein1966binary}. ROUGE-1 precision and ROUGE-L precision measure unigram and longest-common-subsequence overlap~\cite{lin2004rouge}. The primary metric $\phi$ is cosine similarity between unweighted, case-normalized term-frequency vectors~\cite{salton1975vector}, with terms defined by \texttt{[A-Za-z0-9']+}. All reported metrics were recomputed from complete saved text, using independent edit-distance and subsequence implementations checked against dynamic programming. The MAP experiment scores the first heuristic segment's prediction against the entire response, not against an annotated first sentence.

old: The documented pilot recipe reconstructs up to three heuristic segments against the full stored response, although the archived pilot rows do not retain per-sample segment counts.
new: The control experiment reconstructs up to three heuristic segments against the full stored response and saves the actual segment counts and encoder inputs.

old: Pairwise differences in per-prompt $\phi$ were assessed using two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests~\cite{wilcoxon1945individual}. Absolute nonzero differences received average ranks when tied; exact zero differences were removed under the Wilcoxon convention. The implementation applied the standard tie correction to the normal-approximation variance and a continuity correction of 0.5. The effective $n$ was 300 for 20 pairs and 299 for TinyLlama versus Phi-3.5-mini. Holm--Bonferroni correction controlled family-wise error over all $\binom{7}{2}=21$ model pairs~\cite{holm1979simple}, and rank-biserial correlation quantified effect size. Defense--baseline comparisons used the same paired procedure with Holm correction over ten tests. Statistical significance was defined as adjusted $p<0.05$.
new: Pairwise differences in per-prompt $\phi$ were assessed using two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests~\cite{wilcoxon1945individual}. Absolute nonzero differences receive average ranks for ties; zero differences are discarded. The normal approximation uses a tie-adjusted variance and a continuity correction of 0.5, with normal tails evaluated directly to avoid numerical cancellation. Holm--Bonferroni correction is applied separately to 21 model comparisons, six control--true-trace comparisons and ten defense--baseline comparisons~\cite{holm1979simple}; rank-biserial correlation summarizes effect size. Significance denotes adjusted $p<0.05$. A bootstrap interval for a mean difference and a multiplicity-adjusted signed-rank test address different summaries and are not treated as interchangeable.

old: The control and defense pilots derive condition-specific decoder seeds using Python's process-dependent \texttt{hash()} function. The documented \texttt{PYTHONHASHSEED=0} setting provides a reproducible recipe for future runs, but per-sample seeds and an attestation of the historical process setting were not retained in the pilot records. Their exact historical seed values remain unverified. In particular, two archived overhead summaries disagree for \texttt{rand\_pad\_8}, and replaying the seed recipe does not recover either realization. We therefore report its analytically expected overhead, averaging $100\cdot4T_i/B_i$ over the 30 traces of each model, where $T_i$ is the token count, $B_i$ the original payload-byte sum, and $\mathbb{E}[U_t]=4$. This is a distribution-defined cost, not a recovered measurement of the archived padding draws. Deterministic-transform overheads reproduce exactly. The seed-provenance limitation does not apply to the explicit BLAKE2s seed records of the MAP study.
new: The control and defense experiments use explicit BLAKE2s-derived, condition-specific decoder seeds and record every seed and transformed vector. Shuffling uses seed $20260706+17i$ for prompt index $i$. Cross-prompt inputs cycle the trace of donor index $(i\bmod30)+1$ to the target's trace length. Random padding has a separately recorded transformation seed, and its payload overhead is calculated from the actual saved padding realization. These are newly specified pilot random draws, not recovered historical seeds. The control and defense baseline reconstructions use distinct decoder seeds, so even their identical undefended length traces can yield different mean scores. Historical \texttt{hash()}-dependent seeds and inconsistent padding-cost summaries are excluded from the current results.

We therefore report the main campaign as an archived pipeline comparison. TinyLlama and Phi-3.5-mini are retained only as reference-format diagnostics. new: The completed experiments comprise 2100 reconstructions from validated archived length traces, 600 reconstructions of newly generated TinyLlama and Phi-3.5-mini responses, 240 trace-control reconstructions, 360 defense-pilot reconstructions and 3300 MAP reconstructions. Every planned sample is present and independently checked. old: Table~\ref{tab:trace_controls} shows nonzero lexical overlap under all three partial trace ablations. For Qwen2.5-1.5B, the true-trace mean was 0.302, compared with 0.209 for shuffled lengths, 0.107 for a constant trace, and 0.256 for a cross-prompt trace. The corresponding Llama means were 0.291, 0.187, 0.124, and 0.231. The true trace therefore improved mean $\phi$ over the three controls by 0.046--0.196 for Qwen and 0.060--0.167 for Llama. The shuffled condition retains the length histogram and trace length, the constant condition retains the rounded mean and trace length, and the cross-prompt condition retains the target trace length while changing its associated length pattern. The observed gaps indicate sensitivity to these representations, including their effect on segmentation. They do not isolate the contribution of the language prior or eliminate all response-dependent information.
new: Table~\ref{tab:trace_controls} shows that the effect of removing trace features depends on both model and control. For Qwen, the true-trace mean is 0.2904 versus 0.2084 after shuffling and 0.1169 for a constant trace; both contrasts are significant after Holm correction ($p=0.0053$ and $p<0.0001$). For Llama, the true mean is 0.2221 versus 0.1272 for a constant trace ($p=0.0010$). Its shuffled mean is lower (0.1798), but the adjusted signed-rank test is inconclusive ($p=0.2634$). Cross-prompt means are 0.2522 for Qwen and 0.2250 for Llama; neither contrast is significant ($p=0.3625$ and $p=0.8531$). Thus these pilots do not establish a general advantage over unrelated prompt traces. Each control retains some response-dependent information, and transformations can also alter segmentation and encoder coverage.

Estimating information-theoretic leakage would require a defined response variable, repeated sampling and a suitable estimator.

\subsection{Limitations}
Measurement validity limits the main comparison. The archived collector implementation does not preserve all token newline bytes, and its exact historical inputs and version binding are unavailable. Separately decoded token fragments produce visibly malformed references for two models. New hashes of present files cannot resolve either issue. Revalidating the collection path requires archived attacker inputs or new reconstructions from a documented length representation; restoring ordinary decoded references may require new victim generations if the original token IDs cannot be recovered.

The remaining limitations concern scope and uncertainty. The experiment uses an application-layer oracle and does not extract boundaries from TLS, HTTP/2, or QUIC. Victim generation was deterministic; the main table uses one assembled reconstruction per prompt, selecting candidates from three stochastic samples per segment, while decoder-seed variation was measured only for two models and 30 prompts. The 96-token pilots use condition-specific seed recipes, but historical per-record seeds and execution-environment attestation are incomplete. The original prompt-level intervals and tests omit within-scenario dependence; the exploratory analysis of 60 scenario means retains the same significant pairs, but neither analysis resolves measurement errors or decoder-seed uncertainty. MAP calibration and test prompts are disjoint as strings, not as scenarios.

Generation reached the 512-token limit in 34.3--100\% of samples, with no EOS-complete Phi-3.5-mini response. The main campaign reconstructs all heuristic segments, the 96-token pilots allow at most three, and the five-seed study reconstructs only the first; all score against the full saved reference. T5 input and output limits, transform-dependent segmentation, and encoder truncation prevent treating these scopes as matched information budgets. The adaptive procedure is an empirical length inverse followed by the unchanged decoder. Lexical metrics do not measure semantic fidelity or actionable disclosure, and payload overhead excludes SSE syntax, transport headers, buffering delay, and latency. Finally, Gemma-2-2B-it used Hugging Face \texttt{generate()} rather than the one-token loop used for the other six models.

\subsection{Limitations}
The observation is an instrumented log oracle. No packet capture or experiment with TLS, HTTP/2 or QUIC demonstrates that its token boundaries are available to a passive observer. The two historical reference-format diagnostics remain in the archived cohort for traceability, and the other archived references lack original token-ID provenance. Newly generated references are verified for TinyLlama and Phi-3.5-mini, but their configurations are not certified replicas of the historical victim executions.

The primary cohorts use one assembled reconstruction per prompt with three stochastic samples per segment. Decoder-seed uncertainty is evaluated separately for two models and 30 prompts; five seeds are not five independent prompt samples. Scenario bootstrap accounts for grouping within the 60 represented scenarios, without establishing generalization beyond the synthetic corpus. MAP calibration and test inputs are disjoint as exact prompt strings, not as scenarios. Pilot decoder seeds are condition-specific, and their single realizations cannot separate all stochastic variation from transformation effects.

The main archived responses reach the token limit in 34.3--100\% of cases; both historical and new Phi-3.5-mini cohorts lack EOS-complete responses. Reconstruction processes all heuristic segments in the primary and new-reference cohorts, up to three in the 96-token pilots, and one in MAP. All use the full stored response as the scoring reference. Transform-dependent segmentation and the 80-token encoder limit prevent treating these scopes as matched information budgets. The MAP inverse is not end-to-end retraining, and payload overhead excludes transport syntax, buffering delay and latency. Finally, the historical Gemma cohort uses a different victim-generation implementation from the other six archived cohorts.

For reproducibility, a run should be included in comparative analyses only if all required files are present and all internal sample counts match exactly. In the present campaign, the required files were \texttt{config.json}, \texttt{progress.json}, \texttt{samples.jsonl}, \texttt{summary.json}, \texttt{summary.md}, and \texttt{summary\_by\_topic.csv}. Placeholder or partially completed execution folders were excluded from primary cross-model claims.

Table~\ref{tab:run_ids} lists the directories containing the seven archived runs in the artifact repository at \url{https://github.com/jackaugustyn/LLeakM}. File completeness establishes which records enter the tables; it does not establish valid detokenization or a historical code-to-input binding. The retained \texttt{analysis/repro\_manifest.json} describes an earlier 96-token, three-segment configuration and contains stale code and analysis hashes. It is not an attestation of the 512-token campaign. \section{Artifact Provenance and Completed Experiments}\label{app:runs}
The artifact repository at \url{https://github.com/jackaugustyn/LLeakM} separates archived victim responses from the completed reconstruction runs. Table~\ref{tab:run_ids} identifies the original 512-token source directories. Each completed run binds its sample inventory, source hashes, model files, code, seeds and environment to a protocol. All planned reconstructions are present; partial probes are excluded. The \path{inference_validation/} reports and the secondary summary contain the numerical sources for the manuscript, while \path{final_review_20261101/} records the final numerical and manuscript checks.
